strengths: The interactive UI-to-code paradigm is a well-motivated reframing of the task: the argument that one-shot generation is fundamentally limited because pixel-level fidelity is unverifiable without rendering is convincing, and iterative polishing with rendered visual feedback is a natural and practically useful mechanism that enables test-time scaling (Table 2 shows consistent gains from N=1 to N=5 on the real benchmark).

Comprehensive, well-structured training recipe (continual pre-training on ~20M real web pairs, SFT with carefully constructed data, GRPO with a designed verifier reward), covering the full pipeline for a foundational UI coding VLM and open-sourced — a genuinely useful contribution to the community given prior UI coding models are largely unavailable.

Thoughtful RL reward design with an honest, informative ablation: the paper shows CLIP-based rewards actually degrade performance below the SFT baseline (Table 3b) while VLM-based rewards help, and the round-robin comparator addresses calibration drift in a principled way (Algorithms 1-3 are clearly specified).

Construction of two new benchmarks (UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-bench) targeting real-world webpage complexity and the previously unevaluated polishing task, addressing a real gap in existing evaluation; the observation that open-source models fall below 50% on polishing is a useful diagnostic.

Strong empirical results: 9B model surpasses much larger open-source VLMs by large margins and is competitive with leading closed-source models, supported by ablations on real-world RL data (Table 4) and verifier reliability (Table 3a).
weaknesses: Evaluation validity is the central concern: the main metric is VLM-as-judge accuracy (o4-mini for UI-to-code, Gemini-2.5-Pro for polishing) with an arbitrary threshold of 80 (Eq. 3), and the RL reward itself is a VLM similarity score (GLM-4.5V). This creates circularity — the model is optimized against a VLM judge and then evaluated by VLM judges — raising the risk of rewards/evaluations rewarding judge-pleasing outputs rather than true fidelity. No human evaluation on the headline results is reported, despite Design2Code's original paper validating metrics with human judgments.

Potential train/test contamination is not addressed: pretraining crawls ~10M real webpages, and public benchmarks like Design2Code are built from real-world sites; UI2Code-Real is also self-curated from in-the-wild sources with no stated decontamination or overlap check against the pretraining/RL corpora. RL data even includes outputs from the model's own earlier checkpoints, compounding this.

The UI editing capability is claimed as one of three core contributions of the paradigm, but has no quantitative evaluation whatsoever — only qualitative demo cases (A.5.2). This contribution is therefore unsupported by evidence.

Missing comparisons against the agent-based systems the related work itself highlights (ScreenCoder, DCGen, DeclarUI), which currently represent the strongest prior approaches for complex real-world UI generation; the paper criticizes these as 'rigid' but does not empirically compare.

Some reproducibility gaps and internal inconsistencies: the verifier is said to be fine-tuned with SFT but training details are not given; the test-time scaling table has missing entries (N=4,5 omitted for synthetic without full justification); evaluation hyperparameters (temperature, decoding, number of judge calls/variance) are unreported; judge scoring variance and confidence intervals are absent given small benchmarks (~100 samples).

Presentation issues: the abstract appears truncated ('available at' with no URL), some quantitative claims in the intro (e.g., 'advancing the open-source frontier by 35% on average') are not clearly traced to a specific table, and there is no limitations section — notably absent given reliance on VLM judges, potential copyright/licensing concerns from crawling 10M webpages, and the risk of the model generating code reproducing copyrighted site content.

strengths: Ambitious and well-executed engineering: UI2Code^N is presented as the first open-source VLM unifying UI-to-code, UI polishing, and UI editing, and reports results that surpass strong closed-source models (e.g., Claude-4-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro) on multiple benchmarks, which if reliable would be a meaningful contribution to the open-source community.

The full training recipe (continual pretraining on ~20M vision-code samples, SFT on 80K curated samples, GRPO-based RL) is documented with concrete hyperparameters, and the paper claims release of code and models, supporting reproducibility of the system itself.

The reward-design ablations (Table 3) are informative: the round-robin comparator verifier outperforming vanilla verifier scoring, the sensitivity of RL to verifier fine-tuning, and the finding that CLIP-based rewards actively degrade performance compared to VLM-based rewards are useful empirical findings for the broader RL-for-visual-generation community.

The interactive UI-to-code framing (iterative polishing with rendered visual feedback as test-time scaling) is a sensible reframing of the task that better matches real development workflows, and Table 2 shows consistent gains on the real subset from N=1 to N=5.
weaknesses: Evaluation methodology has circularity and reliability concerns. The central metric is a VLM-as-judge score (o4-mini for UI-to-code, Gemini-2.5-Pro for polishing), yet the paper itself demonstrates (Table 3) that VLM judge reliability is fragile—removing verifier fine-tuning degrades accuracy by ~3%, and CLIP-based judgment is 'brittle.' No human evaluation is provided to validate that the judge scores track actual visual fidelity, so the headline SOTA claims rest on an unvalidated automatic metric.

The RL reward objective for UI polishing (relative success criterion: score(A,C) > score(A,B)) is essentially identical to the evaluation metric, creating a strong reward-hacking incentive. The model is trained to please a judge of the same type used for evaluation (and the reward verifier, GLM-4.5V, is from the same family as the base model GLM-4.1V). The paper does not analyze or rule out verifier exploitation, which undermines confidence in the polishing results.

UI editing—one of the three claimed core capabilities—is never quantitatively evaluated. All evidence is qualitative demo figures (Appendix A.5.2), so the claim that the model 'unifies three key capabilities' is only one-third supported by evidence.

The two benchmarks most favorable to the paper (UI2Code-Real with 115 examples, UIPolish-bench with 200) are self-constructed, small, and described only briefly; there is no decontamination analysis showing they are disjoint from the ~10M crawled pretraining pages or the Mind2Web RL data collected 'from in-the-wild sources.' Contamination risk is not addressed.

No statistical rigor: single-run results, no variance/seeds reported, no significance tests, and test-time scaling gains are modest and saturating (66.0→74.0 on UI2Code-Real; synthetic saturates by N=2), making the '12% improvement' claim in the contributions list somewhat overstated.

Key quantitative claims are vague or inconsistent: 'advancing the open-source UI-to-code frontier by 35% on average' is not clearly derived from Table 1, and abstract/figure numbers (e.g., 74.0/94.0 in Figure 1) do not always match table values, suggesting sloppy reporting.

Reproducibility of the full pipeline is limited: SFT data generation depends on proprietary models (Claude-3.7-Sonnet-Thinking), the RL reward depends on GLM-4.5V and its fine-tuned verifier (fine-tuning details sparse), and the crawled corpus construction is described only at a high level.

No limitations section or honest discussion of risks (judge-based metrics, contamination, editing evaluation gap); the 'new paradigm' framing oversells what is essentially iterative refinement with rendering feedback, which has precedents in agentic UI-to-code workflows the paper dismisses fairly quickly.

strengths: The paper makes a substantial and practical contribution: a fully open-source 9B VLM (UI2Code^N) that unifies UI-to-code generation, UI polishing, and UI editing, with results competitive with leading closed-source systems (Table 1), which is valuable for the community given the scarcity of open models in this space.

The proposed Interactive UI-to-Code paradigm is a sensible reframing of UI coding as iterative reasoning with rendered visual feedback, and the test-time scaling results (Table 2, +8 points on UI2Code-Real from N=1 to N=5) provide evidence that the paradigm raises the achievable performance ceiling rather than merely restructuring the task.

The three-stage training recipe (continual pretraining on ~10M noisy real webpage pairs, SFT with carefully constructed reverse-generated data, and GRPO RL on unpaired real data) is described with enough specificity (data scales, hyperparameters, batch sizes) to be genuinely reusable, and the claim that this is the first full training recipe for a foundational coding VLM is credible.

The reward design section is a highlight: the progressive refinement from verifier scoring to comparator scoring to round-robin pairwise comparison (Appendix A.1, Algorithms 1-3) directly addresses known calibration weaknesses of VLM judges, and the ablations (Table 3) support each design choice.

The paper includes meaningful ablations beyond the headline results: the finding that CLIP rewards actively degrade performance versus VLM rewards (Table 3b), and that real-world webpages in the RL stage are critical for bridging the sim-to-real gap (Table 4), are both informative for future work.
Constructing new, more realistic evaluation resources (UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-bench) addresses a real gap, since existing benchmarks rely on synthetic or heavily pruned HTML.
weaknesses: Circularity and potential bias in evaluation: both UI-to-code and UI polishing are scored by closed-source VLM judges (o4-mini for UI-to-code, Gemini-2.5-Pro for polishing), and the RL reward itself comes from a fine-tuned GLM-4.5V. There is no human evaluation on the new benchmarks, so the central SOTA claims rest entirely on VLM-as-judge metrics whose correlation with human judgment on these specific tasks (especially the arbitrary threshold of 80 in Eq. 3) is not validated. The RL model was explicitly optimized against a similar judge, raising reward-hacking concerns that the paper does not test for.

Internal numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results: Table 1 reports UI2Code^N-9B-RL at 76.5 on UI2Code-Real, but Table 2 (test-time scaling, presumably the same model) starts at N=1 with 66.0 on the same benchmark; Table 1 reports SFT at 79.3 on Design2Code while Table 3b reports UI2Code^N-SFT at 72.3. These discrepancies are unexplained and could reflect different checkpoints, but as written they make the headline numbers hard to interpret.

Claim of 'advancing the open-source UI-to-code frontier by 35% on average' is not clearly substantiated by Table 1; the averaging basis (which baselines, which benchmarks) is not stated, and given GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking's already strong baseline (64.7 on Design2Code), the gap between the best prior open model and UI2Code^N appears considerably smaller on some columns.

The base model is an early checkpoint of GLM-4.1V-9B-Base, a strong VLM; while the comparison against other open 9B models is fair, the paper provides no ablation isolating how much of the gain comes from the base model's inherent capability versus the proposed pipeline, and does not report general-capability regression after continual pretraining and RL.

Reproducibility gaps: the abstract's code/model URL is literally missing ('available at' with no link), data licensing for the ~10M crawled commercial webpages is unspecified, and evaluation details such as decoding parameters, thinking budgets, and maximum token limits for the closed-source baselines are not reported — factors that materially affect UI code generation results.

Evaluation sets are small (115 real pages for UI2Code-Real, 100 per UIPolish subset) with no confidence intervals or significance testing, so differences of a few points (e.g., 79.0 vs 78.0 on UIPolish-Real in Table 3a, or 82.4 vs 81.5 in Table 4) may not be meaningful.

The paper has no limitations section and does not discuss ethical considerations around reproducing copyrighted commercial web designs (Amazon, Booking.com, etc.) at scale, or the risks of training on and regenerating scraped web content.
UI editing, one of the three claimed unified capabilities, has no quantitative evaluation at all — only qualitative demo cases in Appendix A.5 — despite being listed as a core contribution.

strengths: The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for a systems paper: results span multiple established benchmarks (Design2Code, Flame-React-Eval, Web2Code) plus two newly introduced benchmarks, with ablations on reward design, training stages, think/answer format, and RL data composition.

Evaluator reliability is treated seriously: the paper reports human-VLM agreement studies at both model-decision and sample-score levels (Pearson 0.93 decision-level, 0.65 score-level), variance/stability analysis over five repeated runs, cross-verification with held-out evaluators (element-matching, CLIP, DINOv3), and a reward-hacking analysis (Table 6 shows the absolute-positioning ratio decreases after RL).

The test-time scaling result (Table 3: performance improves monotonically with refinement rounds on UI2Code-Real) empirically supports the core iterative-refinement hypothesis, and the comparison with agent-based systems (Table 15) shows favorable latency/token cost.

Reproducibility support is strong: detailed training hyperparameters, data composition (CPT ~20M samples, SFT ~80K, RL ~42K), judge prompts, verifier fine-tuning details, and an honest ethics statement with concrete decontamination and PII-filtering procedures.
Training-stage ablation (Table 11) cleanly decomposes the contribution of CPT (+44.3), SFT (+26.0), and RL (+9.3), which helps readers judge where the gains actually come from.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: RVPO is essentially GRPO applied to tournament-aggregated pairwise VLM preferences. Group-relative preference rewards, tournament ranking for RLHF, and preference-based GRPO variants all exist in prior work; the paper does not position RVPO against these closely related formulations or analyze when the tournament reward is a consistent estimator of the expected preference in Eq. 7 (win counts are not unbiased and ignore preference transitivity). The 'interactive visual optimization' framing largely repackages standard iterative refinement plus RL.

The headline claim of 'state-of-the-art ... outperforming substantially larger closed-source models' is overstated. GPT-5 beats UI2Code^N-RL on Design2Code (89.7 vs 88.6) and UIPolish-Real (85.0 vs 80.0), and Gemini-2.5-Pro is essentially tied; the win is limited to Flame, Web2Code, and UIPolish-Synthetic. A more careful, per-benchmark claim is warranted.

The paper is inconsistent about its own method name: 'Relative Visual Policy Optimization (RVPO)' in the abstract and Section 2.3 versus 'Visual Relative Policy Optimization (VRPO)' in the contributions and Section 1. This is a red flag for carelessness in a camera-ready-quality manuscript.

Internal tension in the test-time-scaling narrative: Table 16 shows average polishing accuracy *declining* over polish rounds 1-4 (66.0 → 63.3 → 65.8), which sits uneasily with the claim that 'performance consistently improves with more refinement rounds N'. The stratified analysis (Table 17) partially explains this, but the main-text claim should be tempered.

The central evaluation depends on closed-source VLM judges (o4-mini for drafting, Gemini-2.5-Pro for polishing). The human-agreement studies mitigate this, but the reported accuracy is a thresholded single-judge score (Eq. 19, score >= 80), and no confidence intervals or significance tests are given on the small proposed benchmarks (115 and 100 samples), where the 2.5% granularity makes several claimed gains fragile.

A key missing baseline: test-time best-of-N selection with the same visual verifier applied to a strong off-the-shelf VLM. This would isolate how much of the RL gain comes from RVPO-style optimization versus simply having more compute plus a good verifier at inference time.

The model is described as 'open-source' but is released under a research-only, non-commercial license, and no explicit statement of releasing training code, verifier weights, or data pipelines is given; this weakens the reproducibility claim relative to the framing.

strengths: Comprehensive and unusually thorough empirical validation: the paper reports results across multiple public benchmarks (Design2Code, Flame, Web2Code) plus two newly constructed benchmarks, includes human preference studies (Fig. 5, Tables 7-9), evaluator-reliability analyses (Pearson/Spearman correlations, variance across five independent runs in Table 10), cross-verification with held-out evaluators and metrics (Tables 13, 18), comparisons with agent-based systems (Table 15), and a reward-hacking probe (Table 6).

The test-time scaling analysis (Table 3) and the stratified oscillation analysis (Tables 16-17) are honest and informative, and the oscillation discussion in Appendix G acknowledges quality regressions rather than hiding them.

Reproducibility is comparatively strong: training stages, hyperparameters, data sizes, verifier prompts, and judge-implementation details are provided in Appendices A-B, the verifier's human-agreement is quantified (Table 5), and an open-source 9B model is promised; data governance and decontamination are described in Appendix C.
The framing that rendered feedback supplies a self-verification signal and that one-shot generation mismatches real UI development is well-motivated and clearly articulated.
Ablations isolate reward design (Fig. 3) and real-world RL data (Fig. 4) under controlled budgets, which supports the specific design claims.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core algorithm is a fairly direct combination of known components: GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) with tournament-aggregated pairwise rewards from a VLM judge, which is a well-trodden idea in RLAIF/preference-based RL. The 'interactive visual optimization' formalism (Eqs. 1-5) restates iterative refinement and test-time scaling in optimization language without adding new machinery or theory. The contribution is primarily an engineering instantiation rather than a new method or understanding.

Internal inconsistency that undercuts the central claim. The paper's key motivation is that absolute visual scores are 'noisy, poorly calibrated' and that relative preference is the fix. Yet Appendix A.1 reveals the UI-drafting reward is exactly an absolute GLM-4.5V score (Eq. 16, r = score/100); the relative tournament mechanism (Algorithm 1) is only used for polishing. The main text does not clearly disclose this, so the headline claim 'RVPO ... derives rewards from relative visual comparisons' is overstated relative to what is actually done for drafting.

The core 'relative' reward is itself derived from absolute similarity scores of the fine-tuned comparator (comp_score in Algorithm 1; Eq. 17-18 for polishing), so the claimed dichotomy between unstable absolute rewards and stable relative rewards is blurred; the paper does not clearly explain why fine-tuning the same style of judge resolves the calibration problem it criticizes.

Naming and reporting sloppiness undermines confidence: 'RVPO' and 'VRPO' are used interchangeably (abstract vs. contributions), Table 1 underlines UI2CodeN-RL (88.6) as best overall on Design2Code even though GPT-5 scores 89.7, and Table 16 shows per-round polishing accuracy decreasing (66.0 -> 63.3 -> 65.8), which sits awkwardly with the 'consistently improving' narrative in the abstract and Section 4.2.

Evaluation relies heavily on VLM-as-judge, creating a residual circularity concern even with the mitigations: the drafting evaluator (o4-mini) and reward verifier (GLM-4.5V) are distinct, but both are VLM similarity scorers of the same kind, and the newly proposed benchmarks (115 and 200 samples) are small, author-curated, and scored with threshold-based protocols (score >= 80) that are ad hoc. Human studies cover only 80 samples with two/three annotators.

The reward-hacking analysis (Table 6) examines only one shortcut (absolute positioning at 0.7% -> 0.5%); more subtle visual-reward exploits (e.g., screenshot-like static layouts, decorative fidelity over semantic structure) are not investigated, despite this being a central risk of the proposed objective.

Positioning against related work is thin on the RL side: the connection (and difference) to existing group-relative and pairwise-preference reward methods is not analyzed, and the claim that the paradigm is 'model-agnostic and broadly applicable' is asserted but not demonstrated beyond UI-to-code.

strengths: Well-motivated reframing of UI-to-code as closed-loop, feedback-driven optimization rather than single-pass generation, unifying drafting, polishing, and editing under one formulation.

RVPO's tournament-based relative reward is a sensible, empirically supported solution to noisy absolute VLM-judge rewards; the ablation (Figure 3) directly compares absolute CLIP/VLM rewards against relative rewards under matched RL configurations.

Unusually thorough evaluation: multiple public benchmarks plus new realistic benchmarks (UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-bench), human preference studies against GPT-5/Gemini/Claude, judge–human agreement analyses, variance/stability runs, evaluator-invariance checks, agent-baseline comparison with latency/token costs, and a reward-hacking analysis (absolute-positioning ratio).
Strong practical result: a compact open 9B model competitive with much larger closed-source systems, with clear stage-wise gains (CPT 9.0→53.3→79.3→88.6) documented in Table 11.
Careful ethics/data-governance treatment: robots.txt compliance, PII filtering, decontamination, licensing, and intended-use discussion.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: RVPO is essentially GRPO with tournament-aggregated rewards from a fine-tuned VLM comparator; the 'interactive visual optimization' framing repackages iterative self-refinement plus RLVR. The framing is presented as a paradigm contribution, but the algorithmic delta over standard GRPO+verifier pipelines is modest.

Potential evaluator circularity: the RL reward verifier is fine-tuned from GLM-4.5V using Gemini-2.5-Pro as teacher, while the headline evaluation uses VLM judges (o4-mini for drafting, Gemini-2.5-Pro for polishing). Models optimized against VLM-style visual criteria may be systematically favored by VLM-judge metrics; human agreement (94% on 100 samples) mitigates but does not fully eliminate this concern, and the sample-level alignment is only moderate (Pearson 0.65, Spearman 0.44).

Internal inconsistencies in reported numbers undermine confidence: Table 3 reports N=1 as 66.0 on UI2Code-Real while Table 1 reports 76.5; Table 16 shows polishing accuracy *decreasing* across rounds (66.0→64.7→63.3) while the paper claims performance 'consistently improves' with refinement; the contribution list names 'VRPO' while the method section uses 'RVPO'; Spearman correlation of 1.0 is reported over only 4 baseline points, which is nearly vacuous.

The claim of outperforming 'substantially larger closed-source systems' is overstated: GPT-5 (89.7) and Gemini-2.5-Pro (89.5) still lead on Design2Code drafting, and human evaluation shows substantial tie/loss rates against GPT-5 (27.5% loss) and Gemini (35% loss).

Missing a key baseline for the test-time scaling claim: iterative refinement gains (Table 3) are shown only for their own model; closed-source baselines given the same N-round refinement budget would be needed to attribute gains to the formulation rather than generic self-refinement.

The threshold-80 accuracy metric for drafting is arbitrary and unvalidated against calibrated fidelity; results on the new 100-sample UIPolish benchmarks have wide effective confidence intervals not discussed.

Reproducibility is partial: training hyperparameters are given, but no explicit commitment to releasing code, the reward verifier, or benchmark artifacts is made in the main text; the custom data pipeline (reverse-engineering SFT data) is described only at a high level.
